title: Linear Inequalities, Part 1: The Idea and an Easy Problem

beats.say: A linear inequality is like a linear equation, but it uses a less than, greater than, at most, or at least sign instead of an equals sign.
Its solution is a range of values, not a single number. For example, every number greater than negative four is a solution of x is greater than negative four.

card.text: A range of values, not one number

beats.say: On the SAT, you will solve inequalities, translate words like at most into symbols, and work with systems of inequalities, whose solutions are shaded regions.
Solve an inequality exactly as you would solve an equation, with one extra rule. Multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number flips the inequality sign.
beats.item: Negative multiply or divide flips the sign

beats.say: A compound inequality, such as negative five less than one minus three x, which is at most ten, is solved by doing the same step to all three parts at once.
beats.item: Compound: same step on all three parts

beats.say: In context, the answer is often a whole number. Greatest number of boxes means round down, and least number of trips means round up.
beats.item: Greatest rounds down, least rounds up

beats.say: A point is a solution to a system of inequalities only if it satisfies every inequality in the system, not just one of them.
beats.item: A system solution satisfies every inequality

beats.say: On a graph, y greater than m x plus b is the region above the line, and y less than m x plus b is below. A dashed line means the boundary is not included.
beats.item: Above or below the line; dashed excludes

scenes.title: Words and symbols
rows: at least, no less than, minimum
at most, no more than, maximum

beats.say: Translating words correctly is half the battle. At least, no less than, and minimum all mean greater than or equal to.
At most, no more than, and maximum all mean less than or equal to.
More than, and exceeds, mean strictly greater than, so the boundary value is not included.
Fewer than, and below, mean strictly less than, so again the boundary value is not included.
Why does multiplying by a negative flip the sign? Start with the true statement two is less than five. Multiply both sides by negative one, and you get negative two and negative five.
But negative two is actually greater than negative five, because it is further to the right on the number line. So the sign must flip, to stay true.
Easy example. Solve five minus three x is less than seventeen. The unknown has a negative coefficient, so watch for the flip.
Our plan is to isolate x. First move the plain number, and then divide by the coefficient of x, watching the sign.
Subtract five from both sides. Seventeen minus five is twelve. Subtracting never flips the sign.
Now divide both sides by negative three. This is the step that flips the sign. Twelve divided by negative three is negative four, so x is greater than negative four.

scenes.title: The solution on a number line

beats.say: Let us picture the answer. The boundary value is negative four. We draw an open circle there, because the inequality is strict, and negative four itself is not a solution.
Every number greater than negative four is a solution, so we shade the number line to the right of the circle.
beats.label: x > −4

beats.say: Test a value inside the range, x equals zero. Five minus zero is five, which is less than seventeen. True. Now test a value outside, x equals negative five. Five plus fifteen is twenty, which is not less than seventeen. False.
To recap. An inequality has a range of solutions. Solve it like an equation, but flip the sign when you multiply or divide by a negative number.
beats.item: Flip the sign for a negative

beats.say: At least means greater than or equal to, at most means less than or equal to, and strict signs exclude the boundary.
Check with one value inside the range and one outside. In the next video, we work through medium and hard problems.
beats.item: Check one inside value and one outside
